\begin{abstract}
Trading agents built on large language models (LLMs) act on retrieved news, so an attacker who edits or injects news can change their trades without touching prices or code. We present \rhal{}, a defense layer for such agents and a framework to evaluate it. The layer grounds the agent's reading of the news in market evidence the attacker cannot edit (trailing price features, microstructure proxies and the realized outcomes of similar past windows, all computed without lookahead), and a risk layer then gates and sizes each decision. We test it on a transparent, lexicon-based stand-in for an LLM agent, against an adaptive misinformation attacker in the style of AutoRedTrader and a frozen replay of the same attack, over \val{NseedsRun} paired simulated markets with bootstrap intervals and Holm-corrected tests. Temporal grounding lowers misinformation-driven attack success (net ASR) from \val{CmpNetNone}\% to \val{CmpNetGrounded}\%, a reduction of \cmp{CmpGainAdaptiveGroundedNet}, and by \cmp{CmpGainFrozenGroundedNet} against the frozen attack, at a cost of \val{CmpCostGrounded}\pp{} of clean-market return. Microstructure proxies add no detectable robustness on our synthetic data, and the risk layer's hold-on-conflict rule backfires against the adaptive attacker ($+$\val{CmpGainAdaptiveRiskNetNeg}\pp{}): a defense that reacts to text--market conflict hands the attacker a lever. Placebo controls credit the defense only for what it removes: \val{ShareNoiseOfNaive}\% of the undefended agent's naive attack success (\val{MPlaceboNoneASR} of \val{MInjectedNoneASR} points) also appears when harmless paraphrases are injected. Every no-lookahead guarantee is verified by tests that mutate future prices and text.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
LLM-based trading agents, financial misinformation, adversarial robustness, defense, temporal grounding, red teaming, retrieval-augmented generation, placebo controls
\end{IEEEkeywords}

% =============================================================================
\section{Introduction}
LLM-based trading agents such as FinMem~\cite{yu2025finmem}, FinCon~\cite{yu2024fincon} and TradingAgents~\cite{xiao2025tradingagents} retrieve news from a memory store, reason over it together with market data, and emit sequential trading decisions~\cite{li2025investorbench,zhang2024finagent}. Their text inputs are an attack surface. Unlike a jailbreak, financial misinformation need not cross any safety boundary: a flipped direction word, an inflated percentage or a swapped cause produces text that still reads as plausible news, is hard to flag without a reference~\cite{jiang2026glisters}, and can change what the agent does. Poisoned retrieval corpora~\cite{zou2025poisonedrag} and injected third-party content~\cite{greshake2023indirect} are established threats to LLM applications; trading agents add a direct financial channel.

AutoRedTrader~\cite{liu2026autoredtrader} showed how far such attacks go. Its attacker combines behavioral-bias prompts, minor semantic edits and style rewrites, filters candidates by similarity and detectability, and reinforces the strategies that changed the agent's decisions. In our replication it flips \val{MInjectedNoneASR}\% of an undefended agent's daily decisions. Detecting the edited text is hard~\cite{jiang2026glisters,wang2026life}, and the attacker filters its candidates against whatever detector it faces. AutoRedTrader also proposes a preliminary countermeasure, time-series-informed grounding, which checks news against recent price windows; we develop it into a complete defense layer.

\textbf{Ground the news in evidence the attacker cannot edit.} The attacker controls what the agent reads, not what the market does. \rhal{} therefore places a defense layer between the agent's policy and its orders (Fig.~\ref{fig:harness}). An evidence model summarizes the market up to day $t$ from trailing price features, microstructure proxies and the realized outcomes of similar past windows. Temporal grounding pulls the agent's text signal toward this evidence in proportion to their conflict. A risk layer then gates and sizes the final decision. Every component uses only data available on day $t$, and tests that mutate future prices and text verify this.

\textbf{Evaluate the defense fairly.} Defense comparisons are easy to get wrong: arms that draw different attacker random numbers differ by attack noise alone, an attacker that adapts to each defense shows each one different documents, and adding \emph{any} documents to the agent's pool changes some decisions even when the text is harmless. We therefore trade an attacked agent and a clean twin in lockstep with shared attacker randomness, replay a recorded attack verbatim against every defense in addition to running the adaptive attacker, and subtract placebo controls so that a defense is credited only for misinformation-driven flips. All conclusions are paired over \val{NseedsRun} simulated markets with bootstrap intervals and multiplicity-corrected tests.

\textbf{Contributions.}
\begin{itemize}
\item The \emph{RobustHFT defense layer}: a market-evidence model with leak-free historical analogs, temporal grounding of the agent's text signal, and a risk layer that can only reduce exposure. It works with surrogate and LLM policies (Sec.~\ref{sec:defense}).
\item An evaluation protocol for such defenses: a paired clean twin, common random numbers, adaptive and frozen-replay attacks, a one-step counterfactual ASR, and a placebo-control ladder that separates retrieval noise, bias prompts and misinformation content (Sec.~\ref{sec:protocol}).
\item Results over \val{NseedsRun} markets: grounding cuts misinformation-driven ASR by about \val{RelCutGroundedNet}\% against the adaptive attacker and by \val{CmpGainFrozenGroundedNet}\pp{} against a replayed attack, for \val{CmpCostGrounded}\pp{} of clean-market return; microstructure proxies add nothing detectable on synthetic data; a hold-on-conflict rule backfires; and naive ASR would overstate the misinformation's effect \val{RatioNaiveToMeaning}-fold (Sec.~\ref{sec:results}).
\end{itemize}

% =============================================================================
\section{Related Work}\label{sec:related}
\textbf{LLM trading agents.} FinMem~\cite{yu2025finmem} introduced layered memory and character design, FinCon~\cite{yu2024fincon} and TradingAgents~\cite{xiao2025tradingagents} coordinate multiple LLM roles, FinAgent~\cite{zhang2024finagent} adds multimodal tools, and InvestorBench~\cite{li2025investorbench} standardizes the perception--profile--memory--action design we follow. Finance-specific language models~\cite{araci2019finbert,wu2023bloomberggpt} and retrieval-augmented generation~\cite{lewis2020rag} supply the text channel these agents rely on.

\textbf{Attacks on LLM agents.} Knowledge-corruption attacks inject crafted passages into a retrieval corpus~\cite{zou2025poisonedrag}, and indirect prompt injection hides instructions in retrieved content~\cite{greshake2023indirect}. Automated red-teaming systems search over attack strategies~\cite{zhou2025autoredteamer,jiang2024artprompt}. For trading agents, TradeTrap~\cite{yan2025tradetrap} shows that small textual changes shift decisions, and AutoRedTrader~\cite{liu2026autoredtrader}, the attack we defend against, adds a finance-structured operator space with closed-loop feedback.

\textbf{Defenses.} Detection-based defenses try to flag manipulated text, but reference-free detection of financial misinformation remains hard~\cite{jiang2026glisters,wang2026life}, and an adaptive attacker can filter its candidates against the detector. AutoRedTrader~\cite{liu2026autoredtrader} proposes time-series-informed grounding with 30-day windows and analog outcomes as a preliminary defense. We turn it into a complete layer with leak-free analogs, microstructure evidence and a risk layer, and evaluate each component under adaptive and replayed attacks. Position sizing and stop rules are standard risk controls in trading systems~\cite{lopezdeprado2018advances}; we test whether they also limit misinformation.

\textbf{Financial misinformation and methodology.} Media tone moves markets~\cite{tetlock2007giving} and dictionary methods quantify it~\cite{loughran2011liability}. Behavioral finance supplies the biases attackers exploit: overconfidence~\cite{barber2001boys}, loss aversion~\cite{kahneman1979prospect}, herding~\cite{spyrou2013herding} and noise trading~\cite{delong1990noise}. Negative controls detect confounding in observational studies~\cite{lipsitch2010negative}, and common random numbers reduce the variance of simulation comparisons~\cite{law2015simulation}. Paired bootstrap intervals~\cite{efron1993bootstrap}, permutation tests~\cite{good2005permutation} and Holm's step-down correction~\cite{holm1979simple} support inference over seeds. Lookahead and backtest overfitting are the classic failure modes of trading research~\cite{lopezdeprado2018advances,bailey2014probability}.

\section{Threat Model and Agent}\label{sec:threat}
\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\input{figures/fig_harness.tex}
\caption{\rhal{}. The RobustHFT defense layer (blue) sits between an LLM trading agent and its orders: market evidence that the attacker cannot edit grounds the agent's text signal, and a risk layer can only reduce exposure. For evaluation, an attacked agent (top) and an identical clean twin (bottom) trade the same market in lockstep and differ only in the text they read. MisGen injects edited copies of the day's news and sets a bias prompt in the attacked agent's context. A day on which the two decisions differ is a \emph{flip}; the share of flipped days is the attack success rate (ASR). In the adaptive setting, strategies retrieved on flipped days are reinforced.}
\label{fig:harness}
\end{figure*}

\textbf{Setting and attacker.} Each day $t$ the market publishes a set $\mathcal{N}_t$ of news items about one asset. An agent retrieves the top-$k$ relevant items from the last few days, combines them with market observations, and chooses $a_t\in\{\text{Buy},\text{Sell},\text{Hold}\}$, executed at the next day's open. The attacker can add documents to the agent's news pool and place a behavioral-bias prompt in its context, but cannot touch prices, the agent's code or the clean news. Its goal is to change decisions. Following AutoRedTrader~\cite{liu2026autoredtrader}, MisGen builds each candidate from three operator spaces: a \emph{bias} prompt (overconfidence, loss aversion, anchoring, herding or confirmation); a \emph{minor edit} of one of eight types (direction flip, sentiment shift, numerical, temporal, entity, concept, causal or vague attribution); and an optional \emph{style rewrite} (news or academic register). A candidate is kept only if its TF-IDF similarity to the source is at least $\tau_{\mathrm{sim}}$ and a detectability classifier scores it below a threshold calibrated to a \val{DetFPR}\% false-positive rate on clean text. Strategies are sampled from a P\'olya urn,
\begin{equation}
P(s)\propto 1+\alpha\, h_s,
\end{equation}
where $h_s$ counts how often strategy $s$ was retrieved on a day whose decision flipped~\cite{mahmoud2008polya}.

\textbf{Agent.} Following InvestorBench~\cite{li2025investorbench}, the agent has perception, profile, memory and action modules. Our experiments use a transparent surrogate policy that scores each retrieved document with a negation- and intensity-aware finance lexicon~\cite{loughran2011liability}. It forms a retrieval-weighted text signal $s_{\mathrm{text}}\in[-1,1]$, applies the day's bias as an explicit parameter shift (e.g.\ overconfidence lowers the action threshold, loss aversion amplifies negative signals by $1.7$), and fuses
\begin{equation}
s=\lambda\,s_{\mathrm{text}}+(1-\lambda)\,s_{\mathrm{mkt}},\qquad \lambda=0.75,
\end{equation}
to mimic an LLM's text-heavy reaction. It buys or sells when $|s|$ exceeds $\theta=0.15$, with confidence $\min(1,|s|/2\theta)$. Without the defense layer, $s_{\mathrm{mkt}}$ is only a crude read of the last return and drawdown. A real-LLM policy with identical prompts and cached responses runs in the same harness.

% =============================================================================
\section{The RobustHFT Defense Layer}\label{sec:defense}
The defense layer turns market data into evidence, uses the evidence to ground the text signal, and passes the decision through a risk layer (Algorithm~\ref{alg:defense}). The attacker can edit none of its inputs except the text signal it is meant to check.

\begin{algorithm}[t]
\caption{RobustHFT defense layer on day $t$}\label{alg:defense}
\small
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\Require text signal $s_{\mathrm{text}}$; features $\mathbf{z}_{\le t}$; prices $P_{\le t}$
\State $s_0\gets\tanh(\mathbf{w}^{\top}\mathbf{z}_t)$ \Comment{fixed weights}
\State $A_t\gets$ $k$ windows ending at $e\le t-H$ most similar to the window ending at $t$
\State $\bar r_t\gets\frac{1}{k}\sum_{e\in A_t}\log(P_{e+H}/P_e)$ \Comment{outcomes known by $t$}
\State $s_{\mathrm{mkt}}\gets\tanh\big(0.7\artanh s_0+0.3\tanh(\bar r_t/0.03)\big)$
\State $c\gets 1-\tfrac12\lvert s_{\mathrm{text}}-s_{\mathrm{mkt}}\rvert$ \Comment{consistency}
\State $s\gets\lambda s_{\mathrm{text}}+(1-\lambda)s_{\mathrm{mkt}}$;\ \ $s\gets s-\kappa(1-c)(s-s_{\mathrm{mkt}})$
\State $a\gets$ Buy if $s>\theta$, Sell if $s<-\theta$, else Hold
\State \textbf{if} stop-loss or take-profit is hit \textbf{then return} Sell
\State \textbf{if} $a\neq$ Hold \textbf{and} (confidence $<0.3$ \textbf{or} $c<0.6$) \textbf{then} $a\gets$ Hold
\State $q\gets\min(1,\sigma^{*}/\sigma_{5,t})$, halved if the drawdown exceeds 10\%
\State \Return action $a$ with position size $q$
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

\textbf{Market evidence.} Features are $z$-scored over trailing 60-day windows and clipped at $\pm4$: 1-day return, 5-day volatility, 20-day drawdown, 5- and 20-day momentum, a short-versus-long trend divergence and a residual anomaly. \emph{Microstructure proxies} add a range-based spread~\cite{corwin2012spread}, Garman--Klass variance~\cite{garman1980estimation}, order-flow imbalance~\cite{cont2014price}, volume shock, a high--low range ratio and Amihud illiquidity~\cite{amihud2002illiquidity}. A fixed-weight score $s_0=\tanh(\mathbf{w}^{\top}\mathbf{z}_t)$ (no fitting, hence no leakage) is blended with the outcomes of \emph{historical analogs}: the $k=5$ past 30-day windows whose feature trajectories are most similar (cosine) to the current one. A window ending at $e$ is admissible on day $t$ only if $e+H\le t$, so its $H=5$-day forward return is already known. This is stricter than the common rule $e<t$, which leaks up to $H-1$ days of future prices. The result is
\begin{equation}
s_{\mathrm{mkt}}=\tanh\!\big(0.7\artanh s_0+0.3\tanh(\bar r_t/0.03)\big),
\end{equation}
where $\bar r_t$ is the analogs' mean forward log return and $0.03$ is a typical 5-day move.

\textbf{Temporal grounding.} The consistency $c=1-\frac{1}{2}\lvert s_{\mathrm{text}}-s_{\mathrm{mkt}}\rvert\in[0,1]$ measures how well the news agrees with the evidence. Grounding shrinks inconsistent signals toward the evidence:
\begin{equation}
s_g=s-\kappa\,(1-c)\,(s-s_{\mathrm{mkt}}),\qquad \kappa=\val{Kappa}.
\end{equation}
Text that agrees with the market passes unchanged, while text that contradicts it is moved up to a fraction $\kappa$ of the way toward the evidence.

\textbf{Risk layer.} After the policy, the risk layer can only hold, shrink or exit, never open a trade the policy did not ask for: stop-loss (6\%) and take-profit (12\%) exits checked at the close, a confidence gate (no new trade below $0.3$), \emph{hold-on-conflict} (no new trade when $c<0.6$), volatility-targeted sizing $\min(1,\sigma^{*}/\sigma_{5,t})$ with $\sigma^{*}=1.5\%$ per day, and a throttle that halves the size beyond a 10\% drawdown.

\textbf{LLM policies.} With an LLM policy the layer supplies the same evidence (features, analog outcomes and $s_{\mathrm{mkt}}$) as a structured prompt section, and the risk layer is unchanged. Responses are cached by prompt hash, so runs are reproducible.

\textbf{No lookahead by construction.} Features use trailing windows only, orders fill at the next open, and analogs obey $e+H\le t$. The retrieval TF-IDF and the attacker's similarity filter are fit only on news dated before the evaluation window. Tests multiply all prices after a cut-off by five, or replace every article dated after it, and require bit-identical decisions before the cut-off.

\section{Evaluation Protocol}\label{sec:protocol}
\textbf{Paired simulation.} Every run drives two agents over the same market path (Fig.~\ref{fig:harness}). The \emph{treated} agent reads clean and injected news under the attacker's bias prompt; the \emph{shadow} agent is an identical clean twin. Both have their own portfolio, memory and defense layer, so a flip is a paired, same-day comparison. All randomness flows from seeds derived by hashing (master seed, component, day, item). The attacker is seeded by its injection type rather than by the arm, so every arm of a seed draws the same attacker random numbers: common random numbers~\cite{law2015simulation}.

\textbf{Metrics.} The misinformation exposure rate (MER) is the share of retrieved documents that are synthetic. The attack success rate is the share of evaluation days $\mathcal{T}$ with a flip,
\begin{equation}
\asr=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}|}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\mathbf{1}\!\left[a_t\neq a_t^{\mathrm{clean}}\right].
\end{equation}
\emph{Active} ASR counts only flips in which the treated agent trades. It discounts the defensive Holds a risk layer creates, which plain ASR scores as attack successes.

\textbf{Adaptive and frozen attacks.} In the \emph{adaptive} setting the attacker's feedback loop runs against the defended agent. In the \emph{frozen} setting the attack recorded against the undefended agent, i.e.\ its documents and daily bias prompts, is replayed verbatim against every defense. Differences between frozen arms are therefore caused by the defense alone. Replaying the tape against its own source agent must reproduce that run exactly, and the pipeline checks this on every seed.

\textbf{Placebo controls.} Injecting documents has side effects that have nothing to do with what they say, and a defense should not be credited for removing them. We therefore add the attack's ingredients one at a time on top of identical retrieval, seeds and tapes, so that consecutive differences isolate one component of ASR:
\begin{equation}
\asr_{\mathrm{attack}}=\underbrace{\asr_{\mathrm{plc}}}_{\text{retrieval noise}}+\underbrace{\Delta_{\mathrm{count}}}_{\text{article count}}+\underbrace{\Delta_{\mathrm{bias}}}_{\text{bias prompts}}+\underbrace{\Delta_{\mathrm{meaning}}}_{\text{content}}.
\end{equation}
The \emph{placebo} injects a meaning-preserving paraphrase of every clean item: synonym and connector substitutions that never touch directions, numbers, entities or causes. The \emph{count-matched} placebo paraphrases only the items the attack actually injected, and the \emph{bias-matched} placebo adds the attack's daily bias prompts. All placebo variants draw the same paraphrase for a given (day, item), so each control's pool is a subset of the previous one's. We report \emph{net ASR}, $\asr_{\mathrm{attack}}-\asr_{\mathrm{plc}}$, with each defense's own placebo; $\Delta_{\mathrm{meaning}}$ is the effect of the misinformation itself.

\textbf{One-step counterfactual ASR.} After the first flip the twins' portfolios and memories differ, so later flips may reflect accumulated state rather than the day's text. Each day a throw-away copy of the agent therefore decides with copies of the clean twin's memory and portfolio but the treated agent's documents and bias; cf-ASR is its disagreement rate with the twin. It only reads copies, which a test checks.

\textbf{Statistics.} The unit of replication is a seed, i.e.\ one simulated market with its own news, prices and attacker draws. All arms of a seed share the market path, so every comparison is paired by seed. We report the mean per-seed difference with a 95\% percentile-bootstrap interval ($10^4$ resamples)~\cite{efron1993bootstrap} and a two-sided sign-flip permutation $p$-value (exact for $n\le 16$, otherwise $2\times10^4$ random flips)~\cite{good2005permutation}, Holm-corrected within each family of related comparisons~\cite{holm1979simple}. We call a difference \emph{detectable} only if its interval excludes zero \emph{and} $p_{\mathrm{Holm}}<0.05$.

\section{Experimental Setup}\label{sec:setup}
\textbf{Data.} Each seed generates \val{NDays} business days of synthetic OHLCV from a three-regime Markov drift with GARCH(1,1) volatility~\cite{bollerslev1986garch}, and \val{NewsPerDay} template news items per day about a fictitious company. The items' latent sentiment correlates ($\rho=0.35$) with the next day's return, so news is genuinely but noisily informative. Every template contains an entity, a figure, a cause and a period, so each edit type has a target. The last \val{NevalDays} days are evaluated, matching AutoRedTrader's 60-day window, and the rest serve as warm-up and analog library.

\textbf{Configuration.} Retrieval is TF-IDF top-\val{TopK} over the last three days with recency decay. MisGen uses bias probability $0.7$, $\alpha=1$, $K=3$ attempts, $\tau_{\mathrm{sim}}=0.35$ and one candidate per clean item. Trades pay \val{FeeBps}\,bp fees and \val{SlipBps}\,bp slippage, long-only and without leverage.

\textbf{Arms.} Per seed and defense level (none; grounding with microstructure proxies; grounding plus risk layer) we run a clean arm, the adaptive attack, its frozen replay, and the three placebo controls: 18 paired arms per seed over \val{NseedsRun} seeds. Ablations vary the defense (price-only grounding, microstructure proxies, risk layer alone or on top, without hold-on-conflict), remove one attack component (minor edits, detector filtering, bias prompts, feedback, rewriting), and sweep the retrieval breadth $k\in\{2,4,8\}$ and the grounding strength $\kappa\in\{0.3,0.7,1.0\}$; every ablation arm has its own placebo, and defense and $\kappa$ ablations also face the frozen replay. The full study runs on one laptop CPU core in about 1.5 hours.

\section{Results}\label{sec:results}
\IfFileExists{tables/tab_main.tex}{\input{tables/tab_main.tex}}{}

\subsection{Effect of the defense layer}
Against the undefended agent the adaptive attack reaches an MER of \val{MInjectedNoneMER}\% and a naive ASR of \val{MInjectedNoneASR}\% (Table~\ref{tab:main}); after subtracting the placebo, its misinformation-driven (net) ASR is \val{CmpNetNone}\% \ci{CmpNetNone}. Temporal grounding lowers net ASR by \cmp{CmpGainAdaptiveGroundedNet} against the adaptive attacker (\pholm{CmpGainAdaptiveGroundedNet}) and by \cmp{CmpGainFrozenGroundedNet} against the frozen one (\pholm{CmpGainFrozenGroundedNet}), so the benefit does not depend on the attacker adapting. It also cuts placebo-corrected active flips, the trades the attacker changed, by \cmp{CmpGainAdaptiveGroundedActnet} (\pholm{CmpGainAdaptiveGroundedActnet}). Because each arm is corrected with its own placebo, this gain is not an artifact of grounding making the agent less sensitive to \emph{any} change in its news pool, although it does that too (Sec.~\ref{sec:results-placebo}). The full layer, grounding plus risk layer, lowers net ASR by \cmp{CmpGainAdaptiveGroundedRiskNet} (adaptive) and \cmp{CmpGainFrozenGroundedRiskNet} (frozen): still a large gain, but smaller than grounding alone (Sec.~\ref{sec:results-components}).

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig_frontier.pdf}
\caption{Robustness--return frontier: net ASR under the adaptive attack against the clean-market return of the same defense (mean and 95\% CIs over \val{NseedsRun} seeds). Grounding moves the agent left at a cost in return; microstructure proxies and the risk layer do not move it further.}
\label{fig:frontier}
\end{figure}

The defense does not neutralize the attack: the grounded agent's net ASR is still \val{CmpNetGrounded}\% \ci{CmpNetGrounded}. Its price is \cmp{CmpCostGrounded} of clean-market return, and \cmp{CmpCostGroundedRisk} for the full layer (Fig.~\ref{fig:frontier}). The synthetic news is genuinely informative, and grounding discounts true stories that the lagging market evidence does not yet support. Fig.~\ref{fig:replay} shows one market: under the identical recorded attack, the undefended agent and its twin disagree on \val{ReplayFlipsNone} of \val{ReplayDays} days, and the grounded agent and its twin on \val{ReplayFlipsGrounded}.

Positive is more robust. Rows starting with ``+'' add one component: the proxies to price-only grounding, the risk layer to grounding, and the hold-on-conflict rule to the rest of the risk layer.}

\end{figure}

\subsection{Which components matter}\label{sec:results-components}
\textbf{Price-based grounding does the work.} Price-only grounding alone lowers net ASR by \cmp{CmpAblDefAdaptiveGrounding} (Fig.~\ref{fig:forest}). Adding the microstructure proxies changes it by \cmp{CmpAblDefAdaptiveMicro} (adaptive) and \cmp{CmpAblDefFrozenMicro} (frozen), neither detectable. In our generator, high, low and volume are functions of the simulated return and volatility plus independent noise, so the proxies carry no directional information beyond the price path. Grounding strength matters little: only the step from $\kappa=0.7$ to $1.0$ against the adaptive attacker lowers net ASR detectably (\cmp{CmpAblKappaAdaptiveZeropSevenOnepZero}, \pholm{CmpAblKappaAdaptiveZeropSevenOnepZero}), and each step costs about \val{CmpAblKappaCostZeropSevenOnepZero}\pp{} of clean return.

\textbf{The risk layer can backfire.} On its own the risk layer lowers net ASR by \cmp{CmpAblDefAdaptiveRiskAlone} (\pholm{CmpAblDefAdaptiveRiskAlone}). On top of grounding, however, it \emph{raises} net ASR against the adaptive attacker by \cmpneg{CmpGainAdaptiveRiskNet} (\pholm{CmpGainAdaptiveRiskNet}) and placebo-corrected active flips by \cmpneg{CmpGainAdaptiveRiskActnet}, with no detectable drawdown benefit (\cmp{CmpDdRisk}, \pholm{CmpDdRisk}). The hold-on-conflict rule accounts for the increase: removing it lowers net ASR by \cmpneg{CmpAblDefAdaptiveHold} (\pholm{CmpAblDefAdaptiveHold}). Injected text creates a text--market conflict on exactly the days it is injected, so holding on conflict changes the attacked agent's decision on those days, while its clean twin, reading genuine news, trades as usual. The attacker thereby decides when the rule fires. Against the frozen attack the change in net ASR from adding the risk layer is not detectable (\cmp{CmpGainFrozenRiskNet}).

\textbf{Retrieval breadth.} Net ASR is higher only with the narrowest retrieval ($k=2$ vs.\ $4$: \cmp{CmpAblRetKTwoNet}; $8$ vs.\ $4$: \cmp{CmpAblRetKEightNet}).

\subsection{How much of the attack is misinformation?}\label{sec:results-placebo}
The placebo alone, paraphrases that change no fact, flips \val{MPlaceboNoneASR}\% of the undefended agent's decisions: adding documents reshuffles its top-$k$, near-duplicates displace other items, and decisions near the action threshold flip. The control ladder (Fig.~\ref{fig:decomposition}) attributes the rest. Matching the article count adds nothing detectable (\cmp{CmpDecCountNone}, \pholm{CmpDecCountNone}), the attacker's bias prompts add \cmp{CmpDecBiasNone} (\pholm{CmpDecBiasNone}), and the content of the misinformation adds \cmp{CmpDecMeaningNone} (\pholm{CmpDecMeaningNone}), about \val{ShareMeaningOfNaive}\% of the naive ASR. Naive ASR therefore overstates the effect of the content \val{RatioNaiveToMeaning}-fold, and even net ASR includes the bias prompts.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig_decomposition.pdf}
\caption{ASR decomposed by the placebo-control ladder on the frozen attack (mean over \val{NseedsRun} seeds). Bars sum to the attack's ASR; the article-count component is at most \val{DecCountMaxAbs}\,pp in size and too small to see. Grounding shrinks both the retrieval noise and the content effect.}
\label{fig:decomposition}
\end{figure}

The ladder also shows \emph{how} grounding helps. It lowers the noise floor, cutting placebo ASR by \cmp{CmpPlaceboGrounded}, and it cuts the content effect from \val{CmpDecMeaningNone} to \cmp{CmpDecMeaningGrounded}. Two checks show that these conclusions do not depend on how flips are counted. The one-step counterfactual ASR stays close to the sequential ASR: the gap is \cmp{CmpCfGapNone} for the undefended agent (\pholm{CmpCfGapNone}) and \cmp{CmpCfGapGroundedRisk} with the full layer (\pholm{CmpCfGapGroundedRisk}), so drift between the twins inflates ASR by less than one point. The fully matched counterfactual estimate of the content effect, \cmp{CmpCfMeaningNone}, agrees with $\Delta_{\mathrm{meaning}}$.

\subsection{What drives the attack}
Three attack components detectably raise net ASR (Table~\ref{tab:stats_ablation}): the minor edits themselves (\cmp{CmpAblAttackWoMinorNet}), detector filtering (\cmp{CmpAblAttackWoFilteringNet}) and the bias prompts (\cmp{CmpAblAttackWoBiasNet}), the last consistent with $\Delta_{\mathrm{bias}}$. Without filtering, the first candidate is always accepted, including the causal and vague-attribution edits that the detector almost always flags (Table~\ref{tab:detector}). Strategy feedback and style rewriting raise exposure (MER $+$\val{CmpAblAttackWoFeedbackMer} and $+$\val{CmpAblAttackWoRewriteMer}\pp{}) but not net ASR: with a placebo floor near \val{MPlaceboNoneASR}\%, the P\'olya urn's flip signal is mostly noise, so it learns what gets retrieved rather than what changes decisions.

% =============================================================================
\section{Discussion and Limitations}\label{sec:discussion}
\textbf{Ground in evidence the attacker cannot edit.} Grounding works because the attacker controls the text but not the prices: edits that push the agent against the market's own evidence are exactly the ones it discounts. An attacker that writes misinformation consistent with recent price moves, or that also moves prices, falls outside our threat model and is the natural next test.

\textbf{Do not let the attacker trigger the defense.} A rule that reacts to text--market conflict lets the attacker decide when it fires, and hold-on-conflict raised net ASR in our experiments. Risk rules that key on market state, such as volatility and drawdown, do not give the attacker this lever.

\textbf{Measure defenses against placebos and replayed attacks.} In our setting \val{ShareNoiseOfNaive}\% of the flips that naive ASR attributes to the attack also occur with harmless paraphrases. Defense comparisons should share attacker random numbers or replay a recorded attack: before we keyed attacker seeds by injection type, identically configured arms differed by up to 8.6 points of ASR, more than every defense effect we measured except grounding's.

\textbf{Limitations.} (i)~The agent is a transparent surrogate, not an LLM. The harness runs real LLM policies unchanged, but absolute rates, and possibly the ranking of defenses, may differ. (ii)~Prices and news are synthetic, and injected news never moves prices. In real markets, widely read misinformation can move prices and so weaken price-based grounding; template news is also more regular than real reporting. (iii)~The microstructure null result needs real order-flow data. (iv)~The detectability filter is a small feature classifier (training accuracy \val{DetAcc}) standing in for an LLM judge, and stops are evaluated at daily closes. (v)~Each seed evaluates only 60 days, so we rely on paired differences over \val{NseedsRun} seeds, not single runs.

% =============================================================================
\section{Ethics and Safety}\label{sec:ethics}
This work generates synthetic financial misinformation only to measure and improve robustness. The market and the company are fictitious. Every generated document carries a mandatory provenance label and a safety tag, and generated text never leaves the simulator: our figures and replay viewer show only labels such as edit type, never generated text. The harness has no broker connection or order-routing path, the attacker's objective is decision change rather than profit, and no component disseminates content. We release the framework for defensive research and discourage its use on real news feeds.

% =============================================================================
\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}
\rhal{} defends an LLM trading agent against misinformation by grounding its reading of the news in market evidence that the attacker cannot edit. Over \val{NseedsRun} paired simulated markets with a surrogate agent, temporal grounding cuts misinformation-driven attack success by \cmp{CmpGainAdaptiveGroundedNet}, from \val{CmpNetNone}\% to \val{CmpNetGrounded}\%, against an adaptive attacker and by \cmp{CmpGainFrozenGroundedNet} against a replayed one, for \val{CmpCostGrounded}\pp{} of clean-market return. Microstructure proxies add nothing detectable on synthetic data, and a hold-on-conflict rule backfires because the attacker controls the conflict it reacts to. Placebo controls, shared attacker randomness and frozen replays make these comparisons fair: without them, \val{ShareNoiseOfNaive}\% of the naive attack success would have been credited to the misinformation. Next steps are real-LLM policies, real price and order-flow data, and adaptive attackers that target the grounding signal directly.
